```{python}
import json
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=UserWarning)

POST_DIR = Path(".").resolve()
CLEAN_DIR = POST_DIR / "data" / "clean"
FIG_DIR = POST_DIR / "figures"
STATS_DIR = POST_DIR / "stats"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

with open(STATS_DIR / "summary_stats.json", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    stats = json.load(handle)

df = pd.read_csv(CLEAN_DIR / "main.csv", index_col="date", parse_dates=True).sort_index()

COLORS = {
    "headline": "#e76f51",
    "core": "#1f4e79",
    "target": "#2a9d8f",
    "neutral": "#4a4a4a",
    "light": "#b0b0b0",
}

TWO_PCT_MONTHLY = 0.16515198

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "Calibri",
    "font.size": 10,
    "axes.labelsize": 10,
    "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "xtick.labelsize": 9,
    "ytick.labelsize": 9,
    "legend.fontsize": 8,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": False,
    "axes.linewidth": 0.5,
    "lines.linewidth": 1.8,
    "figure.facecolor": "white",
    "axes.facecolor": "#fafafa",
})


def fmt(value, digits=1):
    if isinstance(value, float):
        return f"{value:.{digits}f}"
    return f"{value:,}"


def fmt_chg(value, digits=1):
    return f"{value:+.{digits}f}"


def fmt2(value):
    return f"{float(value):.2f}"


def extend_xlim(ax, index, pad_frac=0.12):
    span = index[-1] - index[0]
    ax.set_xlim(index[0], index[-1] + span * pad_frac)
```

The Bureau of Economic Analysis said July PCE prices rose **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`%** from June and **`{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`%** from a year earlier. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy, also rose **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_core_mom'])`%** on the month and held at **`{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%** year over year. The yearly headline rate is the same as June. The Fed's preferred gauge did not cool.

Two days later, on `{python} stats['jackson_hole_date']`, Chair Kevin Warsh delivered the Jackson Hole keynote at `{python} stats['jackson_hole_time']`. The `{python} stats['next_fomc_dates']` FOMC meeting and Summary of Economic Projections are still ahead. This post stays with the PCE tables. The speech is context, not the spine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Reproducing this analysis

The Python code for each chart is in this post. Expand any chart block to see the implementation. The pipeline is:

- `scripts/01_fetch_data.py` downloads PCEPI, PCEPILFE, PSAVERT, PAYEMS, UNRATE, DPCERA3M086SBEA, and DFEDTARU from [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/) (requires `FRED_API_KEY`).
- `scripts/02_clean_data.py` computes month-over-month and year-over-year percent changes. Year-over-year means compared with the same month last year. Official July BEA rates are pinned to the release if FRED rounding differs.
- `scripts/03_visualizations.py` writes the five PNGs under `figures/`.
- `scripts/04_compute_stats.py` writes every prose and card value to `stats/summary_stats.json`.

Run the scripts in numeric order from this post folder, then render `index.qmd`. Primary source: [Personal Income and Outlays, July 2026](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Note on data

PCE, or personal consumption expenditures, is BEA's measure of what households spend on goods and services. The PCE price index tracks those prices. Core PCE excludes food and energy. Disposable personal income, or DPI, is income after taxes. The personal saving rate is saving as a share of DPI.

The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is maximum employment and stable prices. The Fed's 2% inflation goal is defined on PCE, not on the Consumer Price Index. CPI is built by the Bureau of Labor Statistics from an urban consumer basket. PCE is built by BEA from a broader set of spending, including more services, and it updates weights with actual spending shares. That is why a CPI print and a PCE print for the same month can differ without either series being "wrong."
:::


Personal income rose **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['pi_mom_pct'])`%**, or `{python} fmt(stats['pi_change_bn'])` billion dollars, in July. Disposable personal income rose **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['dpi_mom_pct'])`%** (`{python} fmt(stats['dpi_change_bn'])` billion). Current-dollar PCE, spending before stripping out prices, rose **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_nom_mom_pct'])`%** (`{python} fmt(stats['pce_nom_change_bn'])` billion). Services spending rose `{python} fmt(stats['pce_services_change_bn'])` billion. Goods spending fell `{python} fmt(abs(stats['pce_goods_change_bn']))` billion. Real PCE, the inflation-adjusted volume of spending, rose only `{python} fmt(stats['real_pce_change_bn'])` billion, under `{python} fmt(stats['real_pce_mom_ceiling'])`% on the month. This post treats that real-spending print as flat. Personal saving was `{python} fmt(stats['saving_bn'])` billion dollars, or **`{python} fmt(stats['saving_rate'])`%** of DPI.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Already on this blog

The funds target is `{python} fmt2(stats['fed_target_lower'])`% to `{python} fmt2(stats['fed_target_upper'])`%. The July FOMC held `{python} stats['fomc_hold']`, with `{python} fmt(stats['july_dissents'], 0)` dissents preferring a `{python} fmt(stats['dissent_hike_bp'], 0)` basis-point increase. July payrolls were `{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_payroll_k'], 0)`k, with unemployment at `{python} fmt(stats['unrate'])`%. July CPI was `{python} fmt_chg(stats['cpi_headline_mom'])`% month over month and `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_headline_yoy'])`% year over year, with core CPI `{python} fmt_chg(stats['cpi_core_mom'])`% and `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_core_yoy'])`%. July PPI final demand was `{python} stats['ppi_print']` on the month.
:::

## 1. The Fed's preferred gauge did not cool

Year-over-year headline PCE stayed at **`{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`%**, the same as June. Core PCE stayed at **`{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%**. June's monthly headline print had been `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_june_mom'])`%. July's monthly headline and core prints were both `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`%. One softer month in June did not pull the yearly rate down.

Headline year-over-year inflation peaked in `{python} stats['energy_shock_month']` at `{python} fmt(stats['energy_shock_headline_yoy'])`% during the spring energy spike. That is the policy-relevant fact heading into Jackson Hole. The Fed's 2% goal is a PCE target. CPI can look cooler, as it did in July at `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_headline_yoy'])`% year over year and `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_core_yoy'])`% core, because the two baskets and the two agencies differ. PCE puts more weight on services that households actually buy, including housing, health, and financial services. Those categories matter more for the inflation the Fed is charged with, and they matter more for property and casualty claim severity than gasoline swings do.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-pce-headline-core-yoy
#| fig-cap: "Headline and core PCE year-over-year inflation both held above the Fed's 2% target after the spring energy spike; endpoint labels show the latest prints."

# YoY means this month versus the same month last year. Rate columns come
# from scripts/02_clean_data.py.
plot = df.loc["2023-01-01":, ["pce_headline_yoy", "pce_core_yoy"]].dropna()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax.plot(plot.index, plot["pce_headline_yoy"], color=COLORS["headline"], linewidth=1.9)
ax.plot(plot.index, plot["pce_core_yoy"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.9)
ax.axhline(2.0, color=COLORS["target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.0, alpha=0.7)
ax.text(plot.index[4], 2.12, "Fed 2% target", color=COLORS["target"], fontsize=8, alpha=0.85)

shock = pd.Timestamp("2026-05-01")
if shock in plot.index:
    ax.annotate(
        "Spring 2026\nenergy shock",
        xy=(shock, float(plot.loc[shock, "pce_headline_yoy"])),
        xytext=(shock - pd.Timedelta(days=220), float(plot["pce_headline_yoy"].max()) - 0.15),
        fontsize=8,
        color=COLORS["headline"],
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["light"], lw=0.8),
        bbox=dict(facecolor="#fafafa", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9, pad=2.0),
        zorder=5,
    )

last = plot.iloc[-1]
ax.scatter(plot.index[-1], last["pce_headline_yoy"], s=40, color=COLORS["headline"],
           edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
ax.scatter(plot.index[-1], last["pce_core_yoy"], s=40, color=COLORS["core"],
           edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
ax.text(plot.index[-1], last["pce_headline_yoy"],
        f"  Headline {last['pce_headline_yoy']:.1f}%",
        color=COLORS["headline"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.text(plot.index[-1], last["pce_core_yoy"] - 0.18,
        f"  Core {last['pce_core_yoy']:.1f}%",
        color=COLORS["core"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="top")

extend_xlim(ax, plot.index, 0.16)
ax.set_title("PCE Inflation Held Above the Fed's 2% Target", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Year-over-year (%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "pce-headline-core-yoy.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) via FRED series PCEPI and PCEPILFE.
:::

**What this chart shows in plain English:** Prices are still rising faster than the Fed wants, and July did not change that yearly picture. Headline and core moved together at the end of the window rather than headline breaking lower. The spring energy spike lifted the headline line; it did not reset the core line to 2%.

## 2. Monthly prints still run above a 2% path

A yearly rate can hide a friendly month. June headline PCE prices fell `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_june_mom'])`%. July went back to `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`% for both headline and core.

A useful benchmark is the monthly pace that compounds to 2% over a year, about **`{python} fmt(stats['two_pct_monthly_pace'])`%** a month. July's `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`% prints sit above that line. One month above the line does not lock in a high yearly rate, and one month below it (June headline) does not lock in 2%. The last 12 months show several readings well above that dashed path, then June's dip, then July back above it.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-pce-monthly-pace
#| fig-cap: "Grouped monthly headline and core PCE changes for the last 12 months, with a dashed line equal to the monthly pace that compounds to 2% a year."

plot = df.loc[:, ["pce_headline_mom", "pce_core_mom"]].dropna().iloc[-12:]
x = np.arange(len(plot))
width = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2))
ax.bar(x - width / 2, plot["pce_headline_mom"], width=width,
       color=COLORS["headline"], edgecolor="white", label="Headline PCE")
ax.bar(x + width / 2, plot["pce_core_mom"], width=width,
       color=COLORS["core"], edgecolor="white", label="Core PCE")
ax.axhline(TWO_PCT_MONTHLY, color=COLORS["target"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.0)
ax.text(
    0.02, 0.92,
    f"Dashed line: {stats['two_pct_monthly_pace']:.2f}% monthly pace that compounds to 2%",
    color=COLORS["target"], fontsize=8, transform=ax.transAxes,
)
ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels([d.strftime("%b\n%Y") for d in plot.index])
ax.set_title(
    f"July's {stats['pce_headline_mom']:.1f}% Monthly Prints Still Sit Above a 2% Path",
    fontweight="bold",
)
ax.set_ylabel("Month-over-month (%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "pce-monthly-pace.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) via FRED series PCEPI and PCEPILFE.
:::

**What this chart shows in plain English:** June's headline decline was real and visible. It did not persist. July put both headline and core back above the slow monthly pace that would, if it lasted, bring inflation in line with 2%. That is a description of one year of months, not a forecast.

## 3. Real spending was flat while saving ticked up

Inflation is the price side. Spending and saving are the quantity and buffer side. Real PCE rose `{python} fmt(stats['real_pce_change_bn'])` billion dollars in July, under `{python} fmt(stats['real_pce_mom_ceiling'])`% month over month. Nominal PCE still rose because prices rose. Households paid more dollars without buying a clearly larger bundle of goods and services.

The saving rate was **`{python} fmt(stats['saving_rate'])`%** of disposable income, up from `{python} fmt(stats['saving_rate_june'])`% in June, with saving of `{python} fmt(stats['saving_bn'])` billion dollars. That is a thin cushion by pre-pandemic standards, even if it is not the lowest reading in this window. Real PCE was `{python} fmt(stats['real_pce_yoy'])`% above a year earlier, so the yearly spending volume is still positive. The monthly print is the cautious one.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-real-pce-saving
#| fig-cap: "Real PCE year-over-year growth alongside the personal saving rate; the latest saving-rate print is marked on the chart."

plot = df.loc["2023-01-01":, ["real_pce_yoy", "saving_rate"]].dropna()
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.grid(False)
ax2.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax1.plot(plot.index, plot["real_pce_yoy"], color=COLORS["target"], linewidth=1.9)
ax2.plot(plot.index, plot["saving_rate"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.8)
july = pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01")
if july in plot.index:
    ax2.scatter(july, plot.loc[july, "saving_rate"], s=40, color=COLORS["core"],
                edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
    ax2.text(july, plot.loc[july, "saving_rate"],
             f"  July saving rate {plot.loc[july, 'saving_rate']:.1f}%",
             color=COLORS["core"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center")
extend_xlim(ax1, plot.index, 0.22)
ax1.set_title(
    f"Real Spending Stayed Soft as Households Saved {stats['saving_rate']:.1f}% of DPI",
    fontweight="bold",
)
ax1.set_ylabel("Real PCE, year-over-year (%)", color=COLORS["target"])
ax2.set_ylabel("Personal saving rate (% of DPI)", color=COLORS["core"])
ax1.set_xlabel("Month")
ax1.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
ax1.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "real-pce-saving.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: FRED series DPCERA3M086SBEA (real PCE) and PSAVERT (personal saving rate); July saving rate aligned to the BEA release.
:::

**What this chart shows in plain English:** People are still consuming more than a year ago, but they barely added any real spending in July, and they are not rebuilding a large rainy-day share of income. Price pressure with flat real outlays is a different story from an overheating boom in volumes.

## 4. Labor context: a weak July jobs print

The dual mandate has an employment side. This blog already covered July's labor data. The PCE release does not redo that analysis. It does sit next to it.

Nonfarm payrolls fell **`{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_payroll_k'], 0)`k** in July. The unemployment rate was `{python} fmt(stats['unrate'])`%. That mix is a softer labor market without a jump in joblessness. For Jackson Hole and for September, it means the price data arrived after a jobs report that already argued against treating the economy as too hot on the employment side alone.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-labor-dashboard
#| fig-cap: "Monthly nonfarm payroll changes as bars and the unemployment rate as a line from January 2025 through July 2026, with the latest payroll decline labeled."

plot = df.loc["2025-01-01":"2026-07-01", ["payroll_change_k", "unrate"]].dropna()
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.grid(False)
ax2.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
bar_colors = [COLORS["target"] if v >= 0 else COLORS["headline"] for v in plot["payroll_change_k"]]
ax1.bar(plot.index, plot["payroll_change_k"], width=20, color=bar_colors, alpha=0.7, edgecolor="white")
ax2.plot(plot.index, plot["unrate"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.9)
ax1.axhline(0, color=COLORS["neutral"], linewidth=0.8)
july = pd.Timestamp("2026-07-01")
if july in plot.index:
    val = float(plot.loc[july, "payroll_change_k"])
    ax1.scatter(july, val, s=40, color=COLORS["headline"], edgecolors="white",
                linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
    ax1.text(july, val, f"  July {val:+.0f}k", color=COLORS["headline"],
             fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center")
extend_xlim(ax1, plot.index, 0.12)
ax1.set_title(
    f"July Payrolls Were {stats['july_payroll_k']:+.0f}k, Unemployment Near {stats['unrate']:.1f}%",
    fontweight="bold",
)
ax1.set_ylabel("Monthly payroll change (thousands)")
ax2.set_ylim(3.5, 5.0)
ax2.set_ylabel("Unemployment rate (%)", color=COLORS["core"])
ax1.set_xlabel("Month")
ax1.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator(interval=3))
ax1.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b\n%Y"))
ax1.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.StrMethodFormatter("{x:,.0f}"))
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "labor-dashboard.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED series PAYEMS and UNRATE.
:::

**What this chart shows in plain English:** Hiring ran hot and then cooled into a July decline. Unemployment stayed near `{python} fmt(stats['unrate'])`% rather than spiking. That is slack opening at the margin, not a recession chart, and it is why the PCE print has to be read beside jobs rather than instead of them.

## 5. The policy rate versus core PCE

The funds target range is `{python} fmt2(stats['fed_target_lower'])`% to `{python} fmt2(stats['fed_target_upper'])`%. Core PCE is `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`% year over year. Plotting those two lines on one axis is a visual comparison of a policy setting and an inflation reading. It is **not** a model of r*, the unobservable neutral real rate, and it is not a rule that says the gap should be a certain number of points.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-fed-funds-core-pce
#| fig-cap: "The federal funds upper bound versus core PCE year-over-year inflation, with the gap shaded. This chart is a visual comparison of two published series. It is not a model of r*, the unobservable neutral real rate."

plot = df.loc["2023-01-01":, ["fed_target_upper", "pce_core_yoy"]].dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.6))
ax.fill_between(
    plot.index,
    plot["fed_target_upper"],
    plot["pce_core_yoy"],
    color=COLORS["light"],
    alpha=0.35,
    label="Gap (not a model of r*)",
)
ax.plot(plot.index, plot["fed_target_upper"], color=COLORS["core"], linewidth=1.9,
        label="Fed funds upper bound")
ax.plot(plot.index, plot["pce_core_yoy"], color=COLORS["headline"], linewidth=1.9,
        label="Core PCE YoY")
last = plot.iloc[-1]
ax.scatter(plot.index[-1], last["fed_target_upper"], s=40, color=COLORS["core"],
           edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
ax.scatter(plot.index[-1], last["pce_core_yoy"], s=40, color=COLORS["headline"],
           edgecolors="white", linewidth=0.8, zorder=5)
ax.text(plot.index[-1], last["fed_target_upper"],
        f"  Funds {last['fed_target_upper']:.2f}%",
        color=COLORS["core"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center")
ax.text(plot.index[-1], last["pce_core_yoy"],
        f"  Core {last['pce_core_yoy']:.1f}%",
        color=COLORS["headline"], fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", va="center")
extend_xlim(ax, plot.index, 0.16)
ax.set_title("Policy Rate Ceiling versus Core PCE (Not an r* Model)", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Percent")
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / "fed-funds-core-pce.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
```

::: {.figure-source}
Source: Federal Reserve (DFEDTARU) and BEA via FRED (PCEPILFE).
:::

**What this chart shows in plain English:** The ceiling on the policy rate and the core PCE yearly rate are both in the mid-3s. The shaded area is just the difference between two published numbers. It does not tell you whether policy is tight, easy, or "right," because that depends on r* and on how financial conditions actually restrain spending.

Chair Warsh's prepared Jackson Hole remarks kept PCE at the center of the price-stability discussion without turning this post into a speech recap:

> "And while this summer's PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved."
>
> Source: [Kevin Warsh, Jackson Hole, 8/28/2026](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm)

That line matches the tables: June was friendlier on the monthly headline, July was not a further cooldown in the yearly rates, and core PCE is still `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%.

## Putting it together

July PCE is a hold-in-place print on the Fed's own gauge. Headline yearly inflation stayed `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`%. Core yearly inflation stayed `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%. Monthly rates returned to `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`% after June's `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_june_mom'])`% headline dip. Real spending was effectively flat. Saving stayed thin at `{python} fmt(stats['saving_rate'])`% of DPI. Services, not goods, carried nominal outlays.

Set beside already-published July jobs, CPI, PPI, and the `{python} stats['fomc_hold']` FOMC hold, the new information is narrow: the preferred inflation gauge did not join the friendlier CPI and PPI headlines on the yearly core comparison. CPI core is `{python} fmt(stats['cpi_core_yoy'])`%. PCE core is `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%. That gap is why this post exists.

## What it means for

**Fed path.** The dual mandate is still split. Payrolls fell `{python} fmt_chg(stats['july_payroll_k'], 0)`k, which weighs on the employment side. PCE at `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`% year over year weighs on the price side. This post does not make a rate call for September. It says only that July PCE did not, by itself, clear the inflation side of the mandate.

**Households.** Nominal income and DPI rose. Real consumption barely moved. A `{python} fmt(stats['saving_rate'])`% saving rate leaves little buffer if prices or hours worsen. Headline PCE at `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`% is still the cost-of-living backdrop, even if gasoline-sensitive CPI looked softer.

**Investors.** The print is not a surprise easing cue and not a new inflation spike. Yearly rates were unchanged. The useful comparison is PCE core versus CPI core, and the calendar into `{python} stats['next_fomc_dates']`. Markets that treated June's monthly dip as the start of a string now have a counter-observation.

**Property and casualty insurers and actuaries.** Services PCE rose `{python} fmt(stats['pce_services_change_bn'])` billion dollars in July while goods fell `{python} fmt(abs(stats['pce_goods_change_bn']))` billion. Housing, health, and financial-services prices sit closer to P&C severity (repair, medical, and claim-handling costs) than energy swings do. A sticky core PCE reading is more relevant to loss-cost trend than a one-month headline dip driven by goods.

## What to watch next

The `{python} stats['next_jobs_date']` employment report is the next labor checkpoint. The `{python} stats['next_fomc_dates']` FOMC meeting includes a Summary of Economic Projections. August PCE is scheduled for `{python} stats['next_pce_date']`. Watch whether core month-over-month stays near `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_mom'])`% and whether the yearly headline rate finally leaves `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`%. One July month will not set the next policy meeting by itself.

## Limitations

Monthly PCE prices are seasonally adjusted and revise. A `{python} fmt_chg(stats['pce_headline_mom'])`% print can be revised away. Year-over-year rates move slowly because they still include last year's months. FRED carried the July 2026 PCE, saving, real-spending, and labor series used in the charts, so this draft does not rely on a reconstructed history. Dollar figures for income, saving, and the goods/services split are taken from the BEA release text. The funds-versus-core chart is not an r* estimate. Chair Warsh's remarks are quoted once from the official transcript and are not a substitute for the tables. One month of PCE does not determine the September decision.

## Methodology and data

| Series or table | Use in this post | Source |
|---|---|---|
| PCEPI | Headline PCE price index, m/m and y/y | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPI) / [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) |
| PCEPILFE | Core PCE price index | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PCEPILFE) |
| DPCERA3M086SBEA | Real PCE quantity index | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DPCERA3M086SBEA) |
| PSAVERT | Personal saving rate | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/PSAVERT) |
| PAYEMS, UNRATE | Payrolls and unemployment | [BLS via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/) |
| DFEDTARU | Fed funds target upper bound | [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DFEDTARU) |
| Personal Income and Outlays | Official July dollar and percent prints | [BEA, 8/26/2026](https://www.bea.gov/news/2026/personal-income-and-outlays-july-2026) |
| Jackson Hole remarks | One short blockquote | [Warsh, 8/28/2026](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/warsh20260828a.htm) |

: Public data used in the analysis.

### How this post was built

Python downloads the FRED series, computes month-over-month and year-over-year percent changes, and writes summary values to `stats/summary_stats.json` so the cards, charts, and sentences use the same numbers. pandas handles the tables. matplotlib draws the five figures. Official BEA dollar figures that FRED does not publish as standalone monthly series are entered from the release and marked in `04_compute_stats.py`.

### Takeaway

July PCE did not cool the Fed's preferred yearly inflation gauge: headline held at `{python} fmt(stats['pce_headline_yoy'])`% and core at `{python} fmt(stats['pce_core_yoy'])`%, real spending was flat, and Jackson Hole opened with that print on the table rather than a new downshift in the trend.
